edges.relationship: In “Worrying about Emotions in History” (2002), Rosenwein challenges Peter and Carol Stearns’s restriction of emotionology to sources and assumptions that marginalize the premodern past.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh OCR reading of the allowed Trieste teaching PDF, printed pp. 824–826: “very shallow past” (824) introduces objections to middle-class advice manuals, excluded courtly literature and premodern childishness. Repairs the held proposal’s unread-page gap. Joint credit to Carol Z. Stearns retained; their originals and Peter’s 1992 review remain unread.

edges.relationship: In “Worrying about Emotions in History” (2002), Rosenwein questions Delumeau’s inference of experienced fear from frightening representations, while praising his range of sources.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh teaching-copy OCR, printed pp. 832–833, especially 833: “from scary sources to real fear?” addresses Delumeau and Peter Dinzelbacher together. Delumeau’s church-centred account is distinguished from Elias’s state-centred account. Sin and Fear and Dinzelbacher’s book remain unread; this is Rosenwein’s objection.
edges.map_label: Questions inference from images to fear

edges.relationship: Rosenwein coordinated the exchange with Patrick Geary, Richard Landes, Amy G. Remensnyder and Timothy Reuter published as “Qui a peur de l’an mil ?” (1999), following their 1998 email discussion.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh primary opening page, Médiévales 37 (1999), p. 15, read through Persée: byline gives Rosenwein “coordination”; introductory paragraph names the four participants, dates the emails 15 January–15 February 1998, and credits her “mise en scène et la mise en forme”. Her opening questions about the millennium were read. This is an undirected editorial collaboration, not sole co-authorship or agreement about the year 1000. Bernadette Grandcolas is credited as translator. Discussion pp. 16–55 and the unabridged emails remain unread.

edges.relationship: Rosenwein and Lynn Hunt co-authored The Making of the West: Peoples and Cultures (first published 2001), as members of a larger author team.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh Rosenwein CV, printed p. 3, “Textbooks”, explicitly says “In collaboration with Lynn Hunt et al.” and dates the original 2001; the distinct Concise History starts in 2003. Loyola’s profile bibliography independently confirms 2001. The publisher’s seventh-edition heading and Authors section confirm joint credit with Thomas R. Martin and Bonnie G. Smith in 2022. Bibliographic collaboration only: no claim about chapter allocation, reciprocal theoretical influence, or the complete first-edition author roster; book body unread.
edges.map_label: Co-authors of The Making of the West

edges.relationship: Alain Guerreau’s 1990 review identifies Mauss’s Essai sur le don as a central resource for Rosenwein’s interpretation of Cluny’s property transfers in To Be the Neighbor of Saint Peter (1989).
edges.evidence_note: Mediated evidence: Guerreau’s own review, printed p. 97, final paragraph, freshly read in Persée’s page-specific text. He names Mauss’s essay as “Le texte capital” for the anthropology of gifts through which she interprets property transfers; Malinowski, Finley, Grierson and Duby also appear as resources. This verifies the reviewer’s attribution, not Rosenwein’s own wording or an endorsement by Guerreau. The book and Mauss’s essay were not read. Page 98 could not be fetched; the rest of the review remains unread. Original 1989 book date is independently listed in the freshly checked Loyola bibliography.
edges.map_label: Gift theory into Cluny property study

edges.relationship: In Donald Wright’s Dictionary of Canadian Biography entry on Creighton (2013), Miller recalls Creighton’s doctoral supervision as prompt and collegial, with suggestions offered as advice rather than instructions.
edges.evidence_note: Read the paragraph beginning “Many of those welcomed into his home were former students” in Wright’s Dictionary of Canadian Biography article (2013). Wright names Miller among Creighton’s doctoral students and quotes Miller’s recollection: “these are suggestions, not instructions”. This is Miller’s testimony as quoted by Wright; the underlying interview and dissertation were not read. 2013 dates the published recollection, not the supervision. No transmission of Creighton’s nationalism or Laurentian interpretation is claimed.

edges.relationship: Coulthard’s Subjects of Empire? (2009) recommends Miller’s Shingwauk’s Vision (1996) as an authority for the history of residential schools while describing exclusion and assimilation before the turn to recognition politics.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading of the University of Victoria repository dissertation: printed p. 5 (PDF p. 13), surrounding argument and nn. 13–15; bibliography printed pp. 232–233 (PDF pp. 240–241). Coulthard discusses repressive state power before the 1969 White Paper, including residential schools; n. 15 recommends Miller’s 1996 book as an “authoritative account”. Note 14 cites John Tobias’s chapter in Miller’s edited Sweet Promises, so that separate argument is not attributed to Miller. Coulthard misstates the book’s subtitle as A History of Indian Residential Schools; the title is A History of Native Residential Schools. This is a named historical authority within Coulthard’s argument, not evidence that he adopted Miller’s whole interpretation, criticized Miller, or derived his theory of recognition from him. The 2014 book and Miller’s book remain unread.

edges.relationship: Trevithick’s 1998 review identifies Miller’s “Reading Photographs, Reading Voices” (1996) as a methodological case for supplementing documentary records with photographs, literature and especially oral history to recover students’ experiences of residential schooling.
edges.evidence_note: Read Scott Trevithick, “Native Residential Schooling in Canada: A Review of Literature” (1998), printed pp. 58–59, with title/issue page and bibliography p. 85, from the institutional I-Portal PDF. On p. 58 Trevithick explains that conventional documentary sources are insufficient for reconstructing students’ experiences and names “pictures, literature, and especially oral history” as Miller’s alternatives. On p. 59 he identifies their use in Shingwauk’s Vision. Bibliography p. 85 dates both works 1996; the later essay collection of 2004 is not their original publication. This is Trevithick’s substantive reading, not a fresh reading of Miller’s chapter or book. It establishes a particular methodological contribution, not priority, universal success, community endorsement, or a general claim about the reliability of oral testimony. No testimony is reproduced. Existing edge_2828 concerns the national synthesis and edge_2829 concerns responsibility; neither has the oral-history endpoint.

edges.relationship: Geary and R. Bin Wong coauthored Societies and Cultures in World History (1994 in Geary's CV), alongside Mark Kishlansky and Patricia O'Brien.
edges.evidence_note: Geary's institutional CV, printed p. 4, Books and monographs: the textbook is listed ‘with Mark Kishlansky, Patricia O'Brien, and Bin Wong’, followed by HarperCollins and 1994. Bibliographic authorship only; textbook body unread and individual arguments unattributed. An indexed publisher advertisement markets a 1995 edition, but its PDF could not be read. The first-publication date discrepancy remains unresolved; 1994 is explicitly the CV's date.

edges.relationship: In “Witch Hunting” (1991), Bartlett criticizes Carlo Ginzburg’s Ecstasies for associating myths across disparate societies without adequate controls and for neglecting their meanings within particular communities.
edges.evidence_note: Primary review read in full on the publisher site. Exact locators: paragraphs beginning “Of course the interpretation of myths” and “Instead of seeking the meanings”, and the concluding discussion beginning “Ginzburg’s poetic intoxication”. Bartlett says “controls are absent” and associations are “entirely subjective”. This records his criticism, not an adjudication; Ginzburg’s book remains unread. See rb_bf_02 for the author’s objections.

edges.relationship: In “The Witches’ Sabbath” (1991), Ginzburg challenges Bartlett’s review of Ecstasies for presenting him as asserting actual nocturnal rituals and embracing Jungian psychology, and for omitting his argument about the medieval construction of the sabbath stereotype.
edges.evidence_note: Primary published letter and Bartlett’s reply read in full. Exact locator: Ginzburg’s four paragraphs under “To the Editors”, especially paragraphs 1–3. He invokes “rituals elude us” and his “explicit rejection of Jung’s approach”. Bartlett disputes these objections in his signed reply. The edge records Ginzburg’s criticism of the review; neither his cited book pages nor the book as a whole was independently read.

edges.relationship: Reviewing Le Goff's The Birth of Europe in 'Off to a Good Start' (2005), Bartlett accepts its account of medieval creativity but insists that eighteenth- and nineteenth-century industrialization and secularization opened a 'great historical divide', and notes that the book steps lightly around the long history of Christian oppression.
edges.evidence_note: Primary review read in full. Exact locators: section 2, paragraphs beginning “Nevertheless, there are fissures” through “We are on one side”, and the final paragraph beginning “Eschewing the Europe”. Bartlett stresses a “great historical divide” and describes Le Goff as “stepping lightly around the long history of Christian oppression”. This appreciative but critical review supplies a bounded disagreement; Le Goff’s book itself remains unread. [Claude verification 2026-10-31, adjusted: NYRB June 9, 2005 review of The Birth of Europe: both locators found. The divide/continuity qualification is well supported. 'Criticizing its treatment of Christian oppression' overstates 'stepping lightly around the long history of Christian oppression', which sits in a closing salute. Narrow that clause.]

edges.relationship: In 'Witch Hunting' (1991), Bartlett cites Keith Thomas's Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971) as the classic example of explaining witchcraft accusations through social tensions and refused neighbourly charity, and accepts its point that poor old women were disproportionately accused.
edges.evidence_note: Exact locator: review paragraph beginning “A classic example of this approach” and its next paragraph. A named explanatory resource in Bartlett’s argument; no general intellectual allegiance inferred. Thomas’s book remains unread. [Claude verification 2026-10-31, adjusted: Passage found. Bartlett presents Thomas as a 'classic example' of the social-tensions approach and partly affirms it ('It does, indeed, seem to be the case that old, poor women... are disproportionately common among those accused'). 'Model' is the researcher's word, not Bartlett's; the next paragraph turns to an alternative (judges' beliefs). Use 'classic example' and state the affirmed finding.]

edges.relationship: In “Alfred G. Bailey — Ethnohistorian” (1989), Trigger criticizes Innis for explaining Indigenous participation in the fur trade through universal economic rationality while neglecting particular beliefs and ways of life.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading of the official Acadiensis PDF, printed p. 5, first paragraph and nn. 7–8 (PDF leaf 3): Innis’s participants become “‘Economic Man’ dressed up in feathers.” Trigger nevertheless credits Innis with recognizing their important role in obtaining furs; n. 8 preserves his acknowledgment of their cultural importance. The note refers back to Trigger’s Natives and Newcomers (1985), pp. 183–184, which were not read. The proposal rests on the 1989 passage, not those unread pages or a claim that Innis simply ignored Indigenous people.

edges.relationship: In A History of Archaeological Thought, second edition (2006), Trigger contests Kuhnian incommensurability and revolutionary replacement as explanations of archaeological theory.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt, pp. 8–9: rival positions are “not incommensurate”; gradual change and recurring positions challenge replacement. He acknowledges Kuhn’s qualifications (pp. 6–7). This reading concerns the 2006 revision; the 1989 first edition is unread.

edges.relationship: In A History of Archaeological Thought, second edition (2006), Trigger criticizes Foucault’s epistemes for underestimating overlap and inadequately explaining archaeology’s simultaneous theoretical diversity.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt, pp. 9–10: “Epistemes can contribute little” to explaining concurrent diversity. He allows potential value. Only this introductory passage was checked; no first-edition attribution is made.

edges.relationship: Reviewing the French translation (1990) of Trigger's Natives and Newcomers (1985) in 1992, Dickason endorses as 'un argument de taille' his warning that excessive reliance on written records distorts Indigenous history, while stressing that archaeological evidence also poses problems of interpretation.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading: Persée HTML p. 284 identifies the translation and original 1985 publication; p. 285, second paragraph, reads “L’auteur invoque un argument de taille” after summarizing Trigger’s warning. The following sentences stress incomplete records and interpretation problems. Page 285 was read in the project’s previously saved official Persée HTML and visually checked against its saved official image. The Sioui discussion begins in the next paragraph and is excluded. Neither version of Trigger’s book was read; this is a bounded review response, not a personal debt. [Claude verification 2026-10-31, adjusted: Persée p. 285 text read directly (not only a saved copy); p. 284 gives 1985 original date. Content of the sentence is supported. Direction/kind is the problem: Dickason did not contribute to Trigger; she received and endorsed his argument. Project precedent for 'X recommends/endorses Y's work' is Y -> X contribution (e.g. edge_2965 james_rodger_miller -> emma_larocque; jrm_bf_02 in this packet). Reverse the direction; sentence can stand.]

edges.relationship: In A History of Archaeological Thought, second edition (2006), Trigger invokes Carr’s argument that selecting relevant evidence presupposes theory against a model of archaeological data collection preceding explanation.
edges.evidence_note: Publisher excerpt, p. 5: explicitly credits Carr (1967: 3–35). A named methodological resource, not mentorship. Carr’s cited edition and Trigger’s first edition were not read.
edges.map_label: Carr on theory in selecting evidence

edges.relationship: In “The Necessity of Atheism” (2017), Brown uses Thomas’s Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971) and The Ends of Life (2009) to challenge assumptions of uniformly religious past societies.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading of the accepted manuscript, numbered pp. 5–6 (PDF pp. 6–7), p. 10 (PDF p. 11), and p. 13 (PDF p. 14). Brown places Thomas at the start of a “sophisticated historiography sceptical of enchantment”, quotes his “continuity of popular scepticism”, and uses his account of practical attachment to earthly life. Notes 18, 22, 40 and 59 identify the works. The 1978 Penguin edition is explicitly identified as a reprint of the 1971 book. Thomas’s originals remain unread; this is Brown’s documented argumentative use, not a supervision or personal-contact claim.

edges.relationship: Brown thanks Richard J. Evans among the readers who read an earlier draft of Postmodernism for Historians (2005) and suggested improvements, noting that not all of these readers endorsed his views.
edges.evidence_note: Licensed preview, Acknowledgements p. vii (PDF p. 8): Evans is among those who “read an earlier draft” and “made suggestions for improvement”. Brown distinguishes advice from endorsement. A bounded manuscript-reading debt; its specific intellectual content is unstated. [Claude verification 2026-10-31, adjusted: Publisher-licensed preview, acknowledgements p. vii; title verso confirms first published 2005 by Pearson, Routledge 2013. The words are '(even when not everyone endorsed my views)', meaning some readers did not endorse Brown's views; Brown is not 'reserving differences of opinion'. Fix the clause. Influence stays bounded to reading a draft.]

edges.relationship: In Postmodernism for Historians (2005), Brown advocates postmodern interpretation while retaining empirical source checking and questioning neutrality in historical narration.
edges.evidence_note: Licensed preview, Introduction pp. 2, 7, 10–11: “Neutrality is impossible” accompanies the requirement to “conduct empirical research”. These primary passages answer the earlier unread-body hold. Chapter 8 remains unread. Existing culture edge_2863 does not state this epistemological position.

edges.relationship: In 'The Agency of Women in Secularization' (2022), a review essay on Philip Jenkins's Fertility and Faith, Brown restates his argument from Religion and the Demographic Revolution (2012) that women's changing fertility choices, higher education, employment and autonomy were central to religious decline from the 1960s, and calls for more attention to the drivers of female employment and the collapse of the ideology of female domesticity.
edges.evidence_note: Accepted manuscript read: unnumbered body, especially PDF pp. 5–6 and 8–9 (PDF p. 1 is the repository cover). On PDF p. 6 Brown relates educational and employment opportunities to women’s movement away from organised religion; on PDF p. 8 he calls for more attention to the “economic, individualistic and cultural drivers of female employment and declining religiosity” and the changing ideology of female domesticity. He critiques and welcomes Philip Jenkins’s Fertility and Faith (2020); Jenkins’s book remains unread. This is Brown’s interpretive argument, not independently established universal causation. Distinct from the existing general methods edge to culture and comparative Canadian religion edge. Repository publication date is 2022; 2021 in the DOI and deposit date is not used as the article’s publication year. [Claude verification 2026-10-31, adjusted: Accepted manuscript (Glasgow repository; cover cites Religion, Brain and Behaviour 12(4) 2022) read in full. The argument is supported, but the piece is a review essay on Jenkins's Fertility and Faith, and the education/employment/fertility argument is Brown restating his own Religion and the Demographic Revolution (dated 2012 in n. 10, 2014 in the text). Say that it is a review essay and a restatement.]

edges.relationship: In “Interview: Steven Shapin” (2025; recorded July 2024), Shapin recalls that reading Rosenberg’s papers on American agricultural research led him to apply to Pennsylvania’s history-of-science programme in the hope of working with Rosenberg.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh primary retrospective testimony: publisher PDF, printed p. 3, paragraph beginning “Only one of my applications”, within the first autobiographical answer (pp. 2–5). Shapin says his reason for applying was reading Rosenberg’s agricultural-history papers; his hope of thesis supervision “didn’t work out that way”. He identifies subsequent friendship and departmental colleagueship. This supports a specific reading-mediated career influence, not doctoral supervision or adoption of Rosenberg’s entire method. The individual papers are not identified here and were not read; their publication years are not inferred. Interview date is on p. 1; original publication was June 2025.

edges.relationship: With Carroll Smith-Rosenberg, Rosenberg’s “The Female Animal” (1973) examines how nineteenth-century medical and biological arguments defended traditional sex roles against women’s demands for education and reproductive choice.
edges.evidence_note: Read the licensed preview of the 1987 anthology From ‘Fair Sex’ to Feminism, chapter opening pp. 13–15 (PDF pages 28–30): https://api.pageplace.de/preview/DT0400.9781135175702_A23800116/preview-9781135175702_A23800116.pdf. p. 13 identifies an analysis of “normative descriptions of the female role”; p. 14 specifies education, birth control and abortion, and medicine’s legitimation of inherited roles. Both coauthors are credited. Publisher metadata and anthology acknowledgements establish original publication in September 1973, not 1987 or the preview’s 2004 reprint. The original journal scan and remaining essay were not read. This is a bounded contribution concerning gender roles, not a claim to found gender history or anticipate its later theoretical positions.
edges.map_label: Medical arguments and traditional sex roles, 1973

edges.relationship: Maier and Niall Ferguson co-edited The Shock of the Global: The 1970s in Perspective (2010), with Erez Manela and Daniel J. Sargent.
edges.evidence_note: Freshly read publisher title page in ETH Library’s four-page front-matter scan, PDF p. 1: “EDITED BY” precedes all four names and the 2010 Belknap Press imprint. Contents on PDF pp. 2–4 allocate separate chapters. Bibliographic collaboration only; the introduction and chapter bodies remain unread. Existing source hc177_ferguson_shock is reused. The Ferguson node already names the collaboration, but neither endpoint has this edge; the four existing Maier edges were checked against the complete graph.
edges.map_label: Co-editors of The Shock of the Global, 2010

edges.relationship: In “Embracing Fearlessness” (2019), J. R. McNeill names Maier among his important graduate mentors at Duke and credits his engagement with twentieth-century European history.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh primary interview, Allison Miller, Perspectives on History 57:1 (January 2019), printed p. 27, PDF p. 29, answer on early mentors: “the most important figures for me were probably Charles Maier” and John Cell; Maier mattered for “the depth of his engagement with 20th-century European history”. McNeill’s own retrospective testimony supports a bounded mentorship/influence edge. It does not identify a formal dissertation supervisor or make Maier the source of McNeill’s environmental method. The subsequent team-teaching and intellectual liberation concern John Cell, not Maier. Printed pp. 26–28 were read through the official issue PDF; the HTML version returned 403.

edges.relationship: Maier and Sven Beckert co-chaired Harvard's Weatherhead Initiative on Global History, founded in 2012; Harvard Magazine (2014) names them as its co-directors.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh institutional About page, “About WIGH”, first and final paragraphs: the initiative “was founded in 2012” by the two historians, who are also named as co-chairs. The dated Graduate Student Presentations programme, 4 May 2015, paragraph beginning “This graduate-faculty research seminar”, identifies History 2950hf, Approaches to Global History, and says discussions “will be moderated by Professors Sven Beckert and Charles S. Maier”. This is a documented joint research/teaching undertaking, recorded undirected; the programme documents announced roles, not a verified transcript of that meeting. No co-authored theoretical position, chapter allocation, or reciprocal personal influence is inferred. The course papers remain unread. [Claude verification 2026-10-31, adjusted: Could not access: both cited WIGH pages (about page and 4 May 2015 seminar programme) return 403 to my fetches, so 'jointly founded' and the 2015 seminar co-moderation are unverified. Allowed alternatives confirm only co-leadership: Queen's University Global History Initiative partners page says WIGH 'was founded in 2012' and 'is chaired by Sven Beckert and Charles S. Maier' (does not say who founded it); Harvard Magazine (Jonathan Shaw, 15 Oct 2014) calls Maier Beckert's 'WIGH co-director'. Narrow to co-chairing and swap the sources.]

edges.relationship: In “Hot Memory … Cold Memory” (2002; delivered 2001), Maier offers a speculative explanation of the differing persistence of Nazi and Communist memories.
edges.evidence_note: New primary evidence for the held memory relationship: online sections I, IV and V, especially the definition, terror comparison and final qualification “very speculative hypothesis”. Western scope; explanatory hypothesis, no ranking of atrocities. Newsletter pp. 1, 5 verifies March 2001 delivery; online footer dates publication 2002. The earlier research statement remains unread.

edges.relationship: In “Hot Memory … Cold Memory” (2002; delivered 2001), Maier tentatively aligns his inquiry with Paul Ricœur’s conference call to move from melancholy to mourning.
edges.evidence_note: Primary section V, final paragraph: Maier names Ricœur’s opening address and suggests his paper contributes to that exercise. Bounded acknowledgment; Ricœur’s original address unread. Newsletter p. 1 independently dates his opening to 9 March 2001.

edges.relationship: In “Military Revolutions, Past and Present” and “Random Thoughts of a Hedgehog” (2003), Parker challenges Black’s organizational explanation and argues that examples of Western military failure do not explain the larger pattern of Western expansion.
edges.evidence_note: Read journal website excerpts, sections under these two titles: opening essay passages containing “Most recently” and “I contend”; rejoinder paragraphs beginning “Jeremy Black’s desire”, “Thus although”, and “Likewise”. Parker contrasts “advances in research and technology” with “military organization”, then argues against Black’s counterexamples. Black’s intervening “On Diversity and Military History” was also read. The website marks omissions with ellipses; complete print essays and Black’s books remain unread. This directed reply differs from Black’s incoming critique.

edges.relationship: In “Homage to Braudel” (1980), Parker criticizes Civilisation matérielle, économie et capitalisme for neglecting war’s economic and social effects and questions whether international trade can bear its explanatory weight.
edges.evidence_note: Read Parker’s own review, London Review of Books 2:17, 4 September 1980. Exact locators: paragraphs beginning “Braudel’s argument will not please everyone” through “But was it really so in pre-industrial Europe?” He finds “no sustained discussion” of war’s consequences and doubts that trade explains European prosperity. Closing paragraphs beginning “In the long term” and “Braudel is a far better historian” retain his high praise. Braudel’s volumes were not read; Parker’s quantitative estimate is not independently verified or adopted.
edges.map_label: War omitted; trade’s explanatory weight questioned, 1980

edges.relationship: In his Itinerario interview (1997), Parker explicitly applies Kuhn’s paradigm concept to explain early modern statesmen’s persistence in policies despite information that contradicts them.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh primary reading in the authorized 2017 reprint, World History – a Genealogy, printed p. 53: after describing selective acceptance of information as “irrational consistency”, Parker names Kuhn’s Structure of Scientific Revolutions and extends the difficulty of recognizing a failed “paradigm” from scientists to statesmen. Note 2, p. 64, cites a 1971 edition. Cambridge’s original-article metadata verifies Itinerario 21:2 (July 1997), pp. 8–19; 2011 is digitization, 2017 the anthology. Kuhn’s book and original journal pagination were not freshly read. Influence means this explicit conceptual application.
edges.map_label: Kuhn’s paradigm applied to policy persistence, 1997

edges.relationship: In “The Crisis of the Seventeenth Century” (Winter 2014), de Vries argues that Parker’s Global Crisis (2013) needs comparative measurement and a clearer distinction between long-term climatic change and short-term weather variability.
edges.evidence_note: Read de Vries’s own review article in the University of Warwick teaching share: p. 372 calls for “comparative and quantitative evidence”; p. 373 considers demographic variation and alternative explanations; pp. 376–377 criticize the substitution of narrative for “measurement and testing”. Pages 369–370 praise Parker’s achievement. Original issue: Journal of Interdisciplinary History 44:3 (Winter 2014), pp. 369–377; the footer’s 2013 copyright is recorded separately. Parker’s book and the demographic data were not independently read or checked.

edges.relationship: McNeill and Carolyn Merchant co-edited the three-volume Encyclopedia of World Environmental History (2003–2004 original edition), alongside Shepard Krech III.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh publisher reading: Berkshire product page, Description, final paragraph, and Additional information, Editor and Copyright rows, names all three editors and dates the copyright 2004. The contemporaneous Routledge launch flyer hosted by Berkshire, PDF p. 4, identifies the same three editors and advertises July 2003; PDF p. 5, About the Editors, confirms their identities. Thus the original-edition year signals differ, and the sentence preserves that 2003/2004 ambiguity rather than silently choosing a year or using a later reissue. JSTOR first-edition book record also gives 2004. The encyclopedia articles and introduction remain unread. This is a co-editing relationship only; no common theoretical position or influence is inferred. Shepard Krech III receives shared credit but has no endpoint.

edges.relationship: McNeill and Kenneth Pomeranz co-edited part 1 of The Cambridge World History, volume VII, Production, Destruction, and Connection, 1750–Present, and co-authored its introductory chapter (2015).
edges.evidence_note: Fresh publisher front matter, ISBN 9781107000209: running header identifies both editors; copyright page, PDF p. 5, visually read, says First published 2015 and separately dates the paperback 2017; Contents, printed p. vii (PDF p. 6), visually read, lists chapter 1, Production, destruction, and connection, 1750–present: introduction, starting on p. 1, under both names. Page 1 of the chapter itself was not read: the starting page is contents metadata, not a claim to have read its argument. Cambridge Core front-matter record for the companion part independently dates print publication 2015. No substantive agreement about global history or causal debt is inferred from the collaboration.

edges.relationship: In Peak Document and the Future of Historical Research (2020), McNeill explicitly borrows vocabulary from James C. Scott’s Seeing Like a State (1998) to warn that scholars simplify other disciplines into usable but misleading forms.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh AHA text: final hazards discussion, paragraph beginning Inadequate appreciation of the complexities of other disciplines, and note 41. McNeill includes himself among scholars who oversimplify other disciplines, calling this an equivalent of seeing like a state. Note 41 states: “This vocabulary comes from James C. Scott,” and cites Seeing Like a State (1998). The following paragraph acknowledges limits imposed by training and finite lifetimes. This is explicit conceptual borrowing in a methodological analogy, not a claim of personal mentorship or that Scott originated McNeill’s environmental history. Scott’s book was not freshly read. The address was delivered 4 January 2020; the existing environmental-history contribution edge does not name this person-to-person resource.

edges.relationship: In the introduction to The Climate of History in a Planetary Age (2021), Chakrabarty uses McNeill’s account of twentieth-century demographic, economic, energy, and resource expansion while connecting capitalist globalization with planetary change.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh licensed Everand preview of the 2021 book: Introduction, Intimations of the Planetary, subsection Capital, Technology, and the Planetary, opening paragraphs, specifically the paragraph beginning As a result of the spread of industrialization and continuing through note marker 8. Chakrabarty explicitly attributes the account to “historian John McNeill” and calls the twentieth century “a time of extraordinary change”; he then moves from the expansion figures to climate justice and the limits of capitalism’s history as an explanation. These are Chakrabarty’s own words, not a publisher synopsis. The preview has no stable print pagination; the numbered note’s text and McNeill work cited there were unavailable, so no identification with a particular McNeill book is asserted. The rest of the book is unread. This records a specific named use, not the origin of Chakrabarty’s planetary framework. The 2009 Four Theses text was separately searched and did not verify this relationship.

edges.relationship: In 'A history of Fear' (2005), interviewer M. O'Connor reports that Bourke cites Eric Hobsbawm as an influence, quoting her praise of historians who 'fuse intellectual rigour with political commitment and verve'.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading of the interview's third web page, section ‘The Second Cold War’, paragraph beginning ‘Amongst the historians’. O'Connor identifies Hobsbawm and Thompson as influences and quotes Bourke praising how they ‘fuse intellectual rigour with political commitment and verve’. This is the interviewer's attribution with Bourke's quoted appraisal, not an invented direct-answer quotation. HTML article:published_time gives 1 May 2005; 29 January 2016 is the modification date. No particular book or transferred concept is specified. [Claude verification 2026-10-31, adjusted: Passage found (published_time 2005-05-01). It is the interviewer's narration ('Bourke cites as influences'), with only the appraisal quoted from Bourke. The relationship sentence puts the identification in Bourke's mouth; label it as the interviewer's report.]

edges.relationship: In 'A history of Fear' (2005), interviewer M. O'Connor reports that Bourke cites E. P. Thompson as an influence, quoting her praise of historians who 'fuse intellectual rigour with political commitment and verve'.
edges.evidence_note: Same freshly read paragraph on web page 3, section ‘The Second Cold War’: Thompson is explicitly named alongside Hobsbawm, followed by Bourke's quoted appraisal of their intellectual rigour, political commitment and verve. The influence attribution is O'Connor's framing of the interview. Original publication is 1 May 2005 in the publisher's HTML metadata, distinct from its 2016 modification. The source establishes a general scholarly influence, not supervision, collaboration or adoption of a specified theory. [Claude verification 2026-10-31, adjusted: Same paragraph as jb_bf_01; the claim reaches us through the interviewer's narration and should be labelled as such.]

edges.relationship: Discussing The Story of Pain (2014) in her 2015 interview with Robin Lindley, Bourke credits Ludwig Wittgenstein's philosophy as helpful for exploring pain's public character.
edges.evidence_note: Interview dated 1 February 2015, answer to ‘You stress that pain is a private and a public experience. What do you mean?’, final paragraph: ‘Ludwig Wittgenstein is extremely helpful’. The preceding answer explains learned cultures of pain. This verifies a named methodological use; Wittgenstein's writings and the full book remain unread. Moscoso's 2015 review independently confirms the book's 2014 imprint and discusses language games, but no specific Wittgenstein text is attributed here.

edges.relationship: Reviewing The Image of Man (1996) in 1997, Bourke argues that Mosse underplays women's and the home's role in making masculine ideals and overestimates postwar youth culture's challenge to them.
edges.evidence_note: Full primary review and appended reply read. Her opening strongly praises the book. Mosse's reply acknowledges the household omission but defends public imagery and greater tolerance. The review dates to 1 February 1997; the reply's displayed 2010 posting is not its established original date. Mosse's book remains unread.

edges.relationship: The Story of Pain (2014), as Bourke explains in her 2015 interview with Robin Lindley, historicizes pain's learned expression and the social inequalities shaping its recognition and treatment.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh primary interview: answers to ‘You stress that pain is a private and a public experience’, ‘How have technical and scientific advances’, and ‘Could you please explain your conclusion’. Bourke describes socialization into pain practices, diminished diagnostic attention to patients' narratives, and unequal relief. Moscoso's review confirms the 2014 publication and the historical scope. Full book unread; this records a contribution to medical history, distinct from existing war, gender and emotions edges, without endorsing clinical advice.

edges.relationship: In “Prejudice behind the pomp and baubles” (2001), MacKenzie argues that Cannadine’s Ornamentalism (2001) underweights racial hierarchies and capitalist interests by concentrating on elite rank and ceremonial display.
edges.evidence_note: Complete review body read on the journal’s own site. Exact unpaginated locators: paragraphs beginning “And this, perhaps”, “There are few testimonies”, “Were they as fascinated”, “Moreover, even if”, “Moreover, when we turn to the workers”, and “There were two imperial hierarchies”. MacKenzie questions the elite source base and stresses racial divisions among workers and economic power outside the honours system. His formulation is “There were two imperial hierarchies”. Closing paragraphs also praise Cannadine: the book “remains an important book”. This is a qualified published criticism, not wholesale rejection. Original review date 27 July 2001; the page’s 2015 update is not its publication year. Cannadine’s book itself remains unread.
edges.map_label: Rank, race and the limits of ornamentalism, 2001

edges.relationship: MacKenzie and T. M. Devine co-edited Scotland and the British Empire (2011) and co-authored its introduction, examining Scotland’s reciprocal relationships with empire.
edges.evidence_note: Licensed publisher preview: title page names both editors; copyright page distinguishes first publication in 2011 from the 2016 paperback. Contents and introduction p. 1 identify both authors. Introduction pp. 1–6 read, especially p. 4 on metropolitan effects and relations among British ethnicities. Acknowledgements p. xv describe the volume as a “collaborative venture”. Contents also credit both for “Scots in the Imperial Economy”, p. 227 onward; that chapter is unread and no claim about its argument is proposed. Edinburgh’s institutional record independently confirms joint editorial credit and 2011. Undirected collaboration, not a claim that either scholar influenced the other.

edges.relationship: Hall, writing with Sonya Rose in “Introduction: being at home with the Empire” (2006), credits MacKenzie’s Studies in Imperialism with changing knowledge of metropolitan imperial culture and cites his argument linking empire to national identity and race-consciousness.

This is named, constructive scholarly reception in their joint historiographical argument; Rose’s coauthorship is essential, although she has no endpoint. It does not establish supervision, personal contact, or exclusive dependence. The original 1999 chapter remains unread. Original year 2001 is explicitly confirmed in Ferguson’s About page, paragraph beginning “The latter won”; the 21 February 2002 date on the book page is the trade paperback date, as identified on the publisher page. Distinct from his existing contribution to the oral-history field and from Sangster’s separate relationships to E. P. Thompson.

edges.relationship: In his contribution to ‘Between Social Scientists: Responses to Louise A. Tilly’ (1985), Thompson defends psychological explanation in oral and social history, arguing that social relationships and psychological states belong together despite weaknesses in existing psychohistory.
edges.evidence_note: Fresh reading of Thompson’s complete individually signed response, original printed pp. 19–21, through the journal’s authorized 2019 supplemental scan; PDF pp. 17–19. Printed p. 21 was also visually checked. In his final paragraph he calls existing psychohistory ‘flat-footed’ but says it addresses ‘a fundamental dimension of human cultural experience’; social relations and psychological states are ‘intimately bound up’. He identifies family relationships, sexuality and the social shaping of personality as historical questions to which oral historians can contribute. The contribution is a defence of these questions within a mixed methodological programme, not an endorsement of every psychohistorical study or a claim to found psychohistory. Although the collective heading names four respondents, the passage ends with Paul Thompson’s signature; the following response is not attributed to him. The original issue is February 1985, not the scan’s 2018 upload or the 2019 tribute. Distinct from edge_2937’s reliability/subjectivity claim and edge_2938’s participation claim.
